entities.summary:
The National Front (Front National) is a French far-right political party founded in 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen — see the entry for 'National Rally' for the rebranded successor. This entry covers the National Front of the United Kingdom, founded in 1967 as a merger of the British National Party and League of Empire Loyalists, which was the most prominent British far-right and neo-fascist organization of the 1970s, notorious for street marches, racial violence, and targeting Black and Asian immigrant communities.

The British National Front (NF) combined fascist ideology, extreme British nationalism, and anti-immigration racism, reaching its peak membership of approximately 17,500 in 1972. The NF organized confrontational marches through immigrant neighborhoods in London, Birmingham, and Bradford — the 1977 Battle of Lewisham, where NF marchers were physically stopped by anti-fascist protesters, was the most significant street confrontation in post-war Britain. The Anti-Nazi League (formed 1977) and Rock Against Racism successfully countered NF's street presence through mass mobilization.

Margaret Thatcher's 1978 television interview — where she said Britain was being 'swamped' by foreign cultures — is credited with absorbing much of the NF's electoral base into the Conservative Party, collapsing NF's vote from 120,000 in 1977 local elections to marginal levels. The NF fragmented in the 1980s; its successor organizations (British National Party, English Defence League) continued far-right activity. The NF represents the British far-right's peak of organized street power before anti-fascist counter-mobilization and mainstream political absorption curtailed it.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The British National Front's 1970s street campaign and the mass anti-fascist response it generated — through the Anti-Nazi League and Rock Against Racism — was the defining confrontation between organized fascism and popular anti-fascism in post-war British history.
